items.title: Level 3: A conditional offer in practice
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: Imagine Priya has just been told she has a conditional offer for an Administrative Officer job. The email says the offer depends on satisfactory pre-employment checks and gives a link to a secure form. Over the next few weeks she fills in the form, uploads her passport and a recent bank statement, lists her last three years of work, and declares that she has no unspent convictions. The checks team then contacts one of her referees to confirm her last job. At each step Priya replies the same day, because delays on her side mean delays to her start date. She keeps a copy of everything she sends. She does not hand in her notice yet. Only when the email arrives saying all the checks are complete and giving a start date does she tell her current employer. This shows how the process normally works. A conditional offer is a real offer, but it is not final. The department can withdraw it if a check is failed, if information is missing, or if it turns out that something on the form was untrue. The checks team are not trying to catch people out. They want to confirm facts so the job can start safely. If something worries you, it is usually best to raise it early with the team. Early conversations leave more time to find a solution, and the team has seen many different situations before.

questions.prompt: What does Priya do first when she gets her conditional offer?

options.text: Waits for her start date before sending any documents
Asks her referees to contact the department themselves
Hands in her notice at her current job straight away
Completes the secure form and uploads her documents

questions.hint: She follows the instructions in the offer email and sends what is asked for.

questions.prompt: Why does Priya reply to the checks team on the same day?

options.text: Delays on her side would delay her start date
Late replies count as a failed check automatically
Replying quickly lets her skip the referee check
The department pays a bonus for quick replies

questions.hint: Quick replies keep the process on track and avoid a later start date.

questions.prompt: When does Priya tell her current employer she is leaving?

options.text: As soon as she has submitted the secure form online
Once the checks team has contacted her first referee and a second one
On the day that she hears she passed her interview
After the email confirms the checks are complete and a start date is set

questions.hint: She waits for final confirmation so she is not left without a job.

questions.prompt: Why does Priya keep a copy of everything she sends?

options.text: So she can pass the copies on to her current employer
So the department does not need to keep its own copies
So her answers stay consistent in later forms
So she can ask for the documents to be returned later

questions.hint: Copies help her keep her answers consistent and give her a record.

questions.prompt: Which of these could lead to a conditional offer being withdrawn?

options.text: The applicant reading the contract before signing it
The applicant asking a question about the process
The applicant taking a week to agree a start date
Finding that something on the form was untrue

questions.hint: Untrue information is a reason to withdraw an offer.

questions.prompt: What is the checks team trying to do?

options.text: Find reasons to turn down as many people as possible
Confirm facts so that the job can start safely
Test how quickly the applicant can answer questions
Decide how much the applicant should be paid

questions.hint: The checks confirm facts; they are not designed to trap people.

questions.prompt: Something in your history worries you. What is usually the best step?

options.text: Ask a friend to describe it on your behalf
Raise it early with the checks team
Leave it off the form and hope it does not matter
Wait until after your first day to mention it

questions.hint: Early conversations leave more time to find a solution.

questions.prompt: Which pair of documents would Priya typically upload?

options.text: A passport and a recent bank statement
A payslip and an old school report
A photograph and a reference from a friend
A CV and a letter from her current manager

questions.hint: Identity and address documents are the usual combination.

items.title: Level 3: Everyday cases for identity evidence
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: The identity check can look different depending on your circumstances, but the aim is always to confirm who you are. A few everyday cases show how it works. Marcus has a full passport, so identity is straightforward, and he proves his address with a recent bank statement. Aisha married two years ago and changed her name, so her passport has her old name. She sends her marriage certificate with it, which links the two names. Leon has just moved house and his driving licence shows his old address. He explains this in a note and sends a recent utility bill with the new address. Kim has never held a passport. The checks team looks at what other documents she has and tells her which combination can be accepted. Documents are checked to see that they are genuine, that they are current and that they belong to the person presenting them. The department compares the photograph to the person, either face to face or on a video call. If a document is lost or stolen, you should report it to the issuer and tell the checks team, because replacements take time. In every case the principle is the same: give the real documents, explain any differences, and ask when unsure. Anything that looks like a changed or false document stops the process, and it can be reported to the authorities.

questions.prompt: How does Aisha show that her old and new names belong to one person?

options.text: She sends a letter from her bank in her new name, signed by a cashier
She sends her marriage certificate with her passport
She sends a new photograph of herself instead of her old passport
She asks her manager to confirm the name change

questions.hint: A marriage certificate links the old name to the new name.

questions.prompt: What does Leon do about his licence showing his old address?

options.text: Changes the address on the licence himself in pen
Explains it in a note and sends a recent bill with the new address
Sends the old licence and says nothing further about the move or the address
Leaves out the address section of the form altogether, to avoid questions

questions.hint: He is open about the difference and supplies up-to-date address evidence.

questions.prompt: What does the checks team do for Kim, who has no passport?

options.text: Looks at what other documents she has and tells her what mix is acceptable
Accepts a written statement from her family in place of any documents at all
Moves her to a different job that has no identity check
Refuses to continue until she has applied for a passport

questions.hint: Other combinations of documents can often be accepted.

questions.prompt: Which is one of the three things the department checks about a document?

options.text: That it was printed on a particular paper
That it was countersigned by a manager
That it is genuine
That it was issued in the same town as the applicant lives

questions.hint: Documents must be genuine, current and belong to the person.

questions.prompt: How is the photograph on a document usually checked?

options.text: By asking a colleague at the front desk whether it looks right to them
By sending it to the applicant's former employer
By comparing it with pictures on the applicant's social media
By comparing it with the person, face to face or on a video call

questions.hint: The photograph is compared with the person themselves.

questions.prompt: One of your identity documents is lost. What is the best step?

options.text: Ask a friend to lend you the same type of document
Report it to the issuer and tell the checks team
Use a photocopy instead and say nothing
Wait for the document to turn up before telling anyone

questions.hint: Reporting early lets the issuer replace it and the team plan around it.

questions.prompt: Which approach applies in all of these cases?

options.text: Give a short written summary of the documents instead of sending them
Give whichever documents are easiest and quickest to get hold of
Give the real documents, explain differences and ask when unsure
Give copies first and originals only if asked twice

questions.hint: Real documents, honest explanation and asking questions are the keys.

questions.prompt: What happens if a document looks as though it has been changed?

options.text: The department corrects the document and carries on
The applicant's referee is asked to explain it
The applicant gets a second try the next day with a new document
The process stops and it can be reported to the authorities

questions.hint: Changed or false documents are treated as serious matters.

items.title: Level 3: Employment history in real life
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: Few people have a perfectly tidy work history, and the check allows for that. Here are some everyday examples. Dana worked for an agency, placed in a different office each month. She lists the agency name and the types of work, and gives the agency's contact details because it holds the records. Omar looked after his mother for eighteen months. He explains this plainly and names his mother's doctor or a family member who can confirm it. Chloe was on a zero-hours contract and sometimes had no shifts for several weeks. She lists the employer and says that her hours varied. Tom spent a year travelling. He gives the countries, the approximate dates and what he was doing, for example short-term work in a hostel. Sam started a course, left after three months and then worked in a shop. He lists the course dates and the shop. In each case, the person tells the truth, fills the whole period and offers someone or something that can confirm it. If the dates are approximate, they say so. If a previous employer has closed or merged, they explain what they know. The department is not shocked by career breaks or short jobs. What troubles it is a history that does not add up, or one that is found to be different from what was written. The shorter and simpler the account, the easier it is to confirm.

questions.prompt: What does Dana give to account for her agency work?

options.text: The agency's name and contact details, plus the types of work
Nothing, because short placements through an agency are not counted
A letter from the last office saying she was a good worker
The names of every office where she sat, with no dates

questions.hint: The agency holds the records, so its details are the best confirmation.

questions.prompt: How does Omar account for the time he spent looking after his mother?

options.text: He leaves the period blank, since it was unpaid work
He says only that he was unavailable for work during that period
He lists a job he might have done at that time if he had looked
He explains it plainly and names someone who can confirm it

questions.hint: Caring is a genuine reason, and a person who knows can confirm it.

questions.prompt: How does Chloe describe a zero-hours contract with weeks of no shifts?

options.text: She lists only the weeks in which she worked
She lists the employer with full-time dates
She lists the employer and says her hours varied
She leaves the contract out because it was irregular

questions.hint: She records the employer and explains the pattern truthfully.

questions.prompt: What does Tom give for his year of travelling?

options.text: The names of the hostels where he stayed overnight
The countries, approximate dates and what he was doing
A statement that time spent travelling is not covered by the check
The full cost of the trip and where all of the money came from

questions.hint: Time abroad should be explained, with an honest summary of activities.

questions.prompt: Why does Sam list the course he left after three months?

options.text: The whole period should be accounted for, even if he did not finish
Leaving a course early is a reason for refusing a job offer
Courses that were not finished earn extra credit towards the checks
The department must contact the course tutor in every case

questions.hint: Every part of the period is accounted for honestly.

questions.prompt: What do these examples have in common?

options.text: The person asks the department to fill in the missing parts
The person lists only the most recent job and leaves out the rest
The person tells the truth, fills the whole period and offers a way to confirm it
The person writes a long story about each job and leaves out the dates

questions.hint: Honest completeness and a way to confirm are shared features.

questions.prompt: What should you say about dates you cannot recall exactly?

options.text: That they are certain, to avoid further questions
Nothing, and use the dates that fit the form best
That they are approximate, and then correct them when you can
That you will provide them once you start the job

questions.hint: Being open about approximate dates keeps your account honest.

questions.prompt: What troubles the department more than career breaks or short jobs?

options.text: A history that includes a lot of part-time jobs
A history that does not add up or differs from what was written
A history that has been confirmed by an agency
A history that includes work in several different sectors and places

questions.hint: Inconsistency is the real concern.

items.title: Level 3: Spent and unspent in everyday terms
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: The rules on spent and unspent convictions can be confusing, so it helps to think of them in simple terms. When someone is convicted, the conviction stays on their record. Over time, if they do not reoffend, many convictions become spent. In most jobs, a person does not have to tell an employer about a spent conviction, and the employer cannot treat it as a reason to refuse to hire them. An unspent conviction, however, is still within its period, and the BPSS asks you to declare it. How long the period lasts depends on the sentence the court gave, not just on the offence. A caution can also have a rehabilitation period. Different parts of the UK have their own rules and their own bodies that provide record checks. A few jobs, for example in policing or working with vulnerable people, are allowed to ask about spent convictions as well, and they must say so clearly. Consider two examples. Ben had a fine many years ago and the period has long passed, so he does not need to declare it for a standard role. Alicia has a recent conviction that is still unspent, so she declares it and gives a short, factual description. In each case the department looks at the facts. It is not a punishment to declare. If you are unsure which category you are in, ask the checks team or an independent adviser before you complete the form.

questions.prompt: What usually happens to a conviction as time passes without reoffending?

options.text: Many convictions become spent
The conviction becomes unspent for another decade
The conviction passes to the next employer
The conviction is deleted from all records at once

questions.hint: With time, many convictions become spent.

questions.prompt: What is the general position on spent convictions in most jobs?

options.text: You do not have to tell the employer about them
You must declare them only if they involve driving
You must declare them if the employer is a government department
You must always tell the employer about them

questions.hint: In most jobs spent convictions need not be declared.

questions.prompt: What does the length of the rehabilitation period depend on?

options.text: The size of the employer
The type of job the applicant wants
The applicant's age at the interview
The sentence the court gave

questions.hint: The sentence decides the period.

questions.prompt: Which sort of job is allowed to ask about spent convictions as well?

options.text: Any post advertised on a government website
Any post in a large private company that deals with sensitive data
Any post that is part-time or based outside London
Some posts in policing or working with vulnerable people

questions.hint: Certain exempt posts can ask about spent convictions.

questions.prompt: Why does Ben not need to declare his old fine for a standard role?

options.text: His employer has already told the checks team
He paid the fine early, so it does not count
The period has long passed, so the conviction is spent
Fines never have to be declared in any job, whatever their age

questions.hint: His conviction is spent, so it need not be declared for a standard role.

questions.prompt: What does Alicia do about her recent unspent conviction?

options.text: Asks a referee to mention it on her behalf, after she starts
Leaves it out because it is only a minor matter
Declares it and gives a short, factual description
Explains it at the end of her probation, if she is asked about it

questions.hint: Unspent convictions are declared on the form, with a plain account.

questions.prompt: How is declaring an unspent conviction treated?

options.text: It is announced to the team you will join before you arrive
The department looks at the facts of the case
It lowers the pay band you are offered, however small the matter
It delays the start date by at least a year

questions.hint: Declaring lets the department look at the facts fairly.

questions.prompt: You are unsure whether your conviction is spent. What is the best step?

options.text: Ask the checks team or an independent adviser before completing the form
Complete the form and say it is spent to be safe
Complete the form and leave that one question blank, to be safe
Wait and see if the department asks about it later on in the process

questions.hint: Getting advice first avoids mistakes.

items.title: Level 3: Right to work in daily situations
items.source: GOV.UK; Home Office right to work guidance
items.body: Right to work checks come up in several ordinary situations. Hannah is a British citizen and shows her passport. The employer copies it and keeps the copy. Niall is an Irish citizen and shows his Irish passport, which is acceptable. Mei holds a visa that allows her to work, but it has an end date. Her employer checks it before she starts and makes a note of the date so it can check again before the visa runs out. Carlos has settled status, which allows him to work without time limit. He creates a share code in his online Home Office account and gives it to the employer, who uses it to check his status online. In all these cases, the employer must carry out the check before the person starts work, and must keep a record. Employers who do not carry out the checks properly can face penalties, so they take the process seriously. It is important to know that the check proves a person's status at the time. If a visa changes or runs out, the person must tell the employer, and the employer must act. The right to work in the UK is separate from the Civil Service nationality rules, which decide who can be appointed to particular posts. Someone can have the right to work in the UK and still not be eligible for a post that is restricted to UK nationals.

questions.prompt: What does the employer do with the passport Hannah shows?

options.text: Posts it to the Home Office for a second opinion
Copies it and keeps the copy as a record
Keeps the original until her first pay day
Asks Hannah to bring it back every year

questions.hint: Employers keep a copy as a record of the check.

questions.prompt: Which document does Niall use to prove his right to work?

options.text: A UK driving licence
His Irish passport
A European health card
A letter from the Irish embassy

questions.hint: An Irish passport is acceptable proof of the right to work.

questions.prompt: What does Mei's employer do about the end date on her visa?

options.text: Asks her to apply for a different visa before starting
Ends her contract on that date without further checks
Ignores the date until Mei mentions it herself near the end
Notes the date so it can check again before the visa runs out

questions.hint: Time-limited permission needs a follow-up check.

questions.prompt: How does Carlos prove his right to work?

options.text: He creates a share code and the employer checks his status online
He asks the Home Office to phone his manager and confirm his status
He brings a letter from a previous employer confirming his status
He posts a copy of his visa to the employer for them to keep

questions.hint: A share code lets the employer see his status online.

questions.prompt: When must the employer complete the right to work check?

options.text: Within the first month of employment
At the first annual review
After the first pay day
Before the person starts work

questions.hint: Checks must be done before the person starts.

questions.prompt: Why do employers take right to work checks seriously?

options.text: Checks are needed to open a staff bank account
Checks are used to decide each person's pay
Employers who do not do them properly can face penalties
Employees can be fined for any delay in starting

questions.hint: The law places penalties on employers who get this wrong.

questions.prompt: A person's visa changes or runs out. What is the right step?

options.text: Tell the employer, who must then act
Tell the bank before you tell the employer
Wait to be asked at the next check, which may be months away
Show the old visa and say nothing about the change

questions.hint: The person must tell the employer of any change.

questions.prompt: Which statement about right to work and nationality rules is correct?

options.text: The right to work makes a person eligible for every post
The nationality rules replace the right to work check
Someone can have the right to work and still not be eligible for a restricted post
The nationality rules apply only after the first year

questions.hint: They are two separate things.

items.title: Level 3: Reading adverts for eligibility
items.body: Learning to read eligibility statements saves time and avoids disappointment. A statement might say that the job is open to UK nationals only. This is the narrowest option. Another might say that the job is open to UK nationals and to certain other groups, such as Commonwealth or Irish citizens, and to people with particular immigration permissions. A third might say that it is open to anyone who has the right to work in the UK. Read the exact words and do not assume. Some statements mention a security clearance level and a minimum period of UK residence for that level. If you have lived abroad recently, that matters. The statement may refer you to a page with more detail on the nationality rules. Take two examples. Jamal is a British citizen with a short stay abroad five years ago. He reads that an Administrative Officer job needs only the BPSS and is open to UK nationals and others. He is eligible. Ellen holds a work visa. She sees a job reserved for UK nationals because of the nature of its work, so she cannot be appointed to it, however good her application would be. She looks for similar jobs where her status is allowed. If you are not sure how a statement applies to you, contact the person named in the advert before you spend time on an application. The answer is usually short and clear.

questions.prompt: Which type of eligibility statement is the narrowest?

options.text: Open to UK, Commonwealth and Irish citizens
Open to anyone with the right to work in the UK
Open to UK nationals only
Open to people with certain immigration permissions

questions.hint: UK nationals only is the most restrictive.

questions.prompt: Why should you read the exact words of the statement?

options.text: The wording is the same in every advert across the Civil Service
Departments ignore the statement when they shortlist
Different adverts name different groups, so you should not assume
The statement is written in a legal style that few can follow

questions.hint: Different adverts name different groups, so exact wording matters.

questions.prompt: What else may a statement mention for roles that need clearance?

options.text: A list of countries you must not visit while you are being vetted
The date of your first security interview
A clearance level and a minimum period of UK residence
The name of the vetting officer who will deal with your case

questions.hint: Statements can state the clearance level and any residence requirement.

questions.prompt: Why is Jamal eligible for the Administrative Officer job?

options.text: The department makes exceptions for people who studied abroad
His time abroad counts as relevant experience
Jobs at this grade have no eligibility rules
The job needs only the BPSS and is open to UK nationals

questions.hint: His status matches the advert and no higher clearance is needed.

questions.prompt: Why can Ellen not be appointed to the reserved job?

options.text: Her application was not strong enough for the role
Work visas are not valid for any government job at all
The job is restricted to UK nationals because of the nature of the work
The job is only open to people who live in London

questions.hint: Reserved posts exclude people who are not UK nationals.

questions.prompt: What does Ellen sensibly do next?

options.text: Applies anyway in case an exception is made for her
Looks for similar jobs where her status is allowed
Asks a friend to apply on her behalf instead
Waits until the same job is advertised again

questions.hint: She looks for roles whose rules fit her situation.

questions.prompt: Who should you contact if a statement is unclear?

options.text: The local job centre where you registered before
Your previous employer, who gave you a reference
The head of the department who runs the recruitment
The person named in the advert

questions.hint: The contact in the advert can explain how it applies.

questions.prompt: When is the best time to ask about your eligibility?

options.text: After you receive an offer of the job
On your first day in the post
After you have been shortlisted for interview
Before you spend time on an application

questions.hint: Asking early saves wasted effort.

items.title: Level 3: Which roles need which check
items.body: The check a role needs depends on the work, not the job title or grade. Most Administrative Officer roles deal with OFFICIAL information such as correspondence, case files and customer details, and need only the BPSS. Some, however, sit in a more sensitive setting. A few everyday examples show how it works. Nina handles customer letters in a benefits centre. Her role needs the BPSS. Tariq is an administrator in a team that supports a police force, with regular access to sensitive operational material, so his role might need a higher level, for example CTC or SC, depending on what he sees. Olivia works at the front desk of a government building that is a possible terrorist target, and her role may need a Counter-Terrorist Check. Raj supports a senior leader who sees SECRET material regularly, so his role may need a Security Check. Developed Vetting is much rarer and goes with the most sensitive roles. The department decides the level in advance and puts it in the advert. It cannot be negotiated, and an applicant cannot choose to do a higher or lower level. If you take a job and later move to a more sensitive one, the new role may need a higher level and you would then need to go through the extra checks. Clearance is always linked to the work, so it is rarely a reflection on the individual.

questions.prompt: What does the check a role needs depend on?

options.text: The sensitivity of the work
The age of the post-holder
The size of the team you will join
The grade of the job that is on offer

questions.hint: The work decides the check, not the grade.

questions.prompt: Which check does Nina's customer letters role need?

options.text: Security Check
Developed Vetting
Counter-Terrorist Check
The BPSS

questions.hint: Her role deals with OFFICIAL material and needs only the BPSS.

questions.prompt: Why might Tariq's role need a higher level such as CTC or SC?

options.text: He regularly sees sensitive operational material
He has been in the Civil Service for a long time
He works in an office outside London
He works part time at a police station

questions.hint: The sensitivity of what he sees drives the level.

questions.prompt: Which check might Olivia's front desk role need?

options.text: Counter-Terrorist Check
Only the baseline checks
A medical check
Developed Vetting

questions.hint: Roles at buildings at risk from terrorism may need a CTC.

questions.prompt: Which check might Raj's role need?

options.text: The BPSS only
A driving licence check
A basic criminal record check only
Security Check

questions.hint: Regular access to SECRET material usually goes with SC.

questions.prompt: How common is Developed Vetting?

options.text: Needed by all staff based in London and the South East
Much rarer, and linked to the most sensitive roles
Needed by most Administrative Officers in the Civil Service
Needed by all managers in the department

questions.hint: DV is reserved for the most sensitive roles.

questions.prompt: Who decides the level of clearance a role needs?

options.text: The department, which states it in the advert
The applicant, who chooses a level
The line manager, on the first day
The vetting team, after the person has started

questions.hint: The department sets the level in advance.

questions.prompt: What can happen if you later move to a more sensitive role?

options.text: Your pay is cut until the checks are finished
The new role may need a higher level and extra checks
You keep your old level and no more checks are needed
Your clearance ends and you must leave the department

questions.hint: A more sensitive role may need a higher level.

items.title: Level 3: Waiting for clearance
items.body: Waiting for clearance can be frustrating, so it helps to know what is normal. After the department sponsors you, UKSV sends you a security questionnaire. Filling it in completely is the single most useful thing you can do. Incomplete forms are sent back, which adds weeks. Vetting teams may also ask for extra information or ask you to explain something, and quick replies help. Clearance often takes weeks and, at higher levels, months. During that time you should keep your current job unless you have confirmation that you can start. Keep your contact details up to date, so that you do not miss a message. Check your email and post regularly, including your junk folder. Do not chase the vetting team daily, as this slows everyone down. If you are worried about the delay, ask your department's security contact, who can find out the status. You should not discuss the details of your vetting with people who do not need to know, such as on social media, and you should not share the questionnaire with others. Some departments allow a person to start in a role with limited access while they wait, but this is not guaranteed and depends on the post. If your circumstances change while you wait, for example you move house or start a new relationship, tell your department's security contact so the information can be updated. It is better to mention it than to have it found.

questions.prompt: What is the most useful thing to do after receiving the questionnaire?

options.text: Skip any parts that you find difficult
Wait until the vetting team contacts you
Fill it in quickly with short answers
Fill it in completely

questions.hint: Incomplete forms are sent back and add weeks.

questions.prompt: What happens to an incomplete form?

options.text: It is ignored and the clearance is granted anyway
It is passed to your referees to complete
It is accepted and finished by the vetting team
It is sent back, which adds weeks

questions.hint: Incomplete forms delay the process.

questions.prompt: How long can clearance take at higher levels?

options.text: Never more than a fortnight
Exactly seven days
Months
Hours

questions.hint: Higher levels can take months.

questions.prompt: What is sensible to do with your current job while you wait?

options.text: Resign as soon as you receive the questionnaire from the vetting team
Keep it until you have confirmation that you can start
Move to part-time hours in your current job to prepare
Resign once you have returned the questionnaire to the vetting team

questions.hint: Do not resign until you have confirmation.

questions.prompt: Why should you check your email, post and junk folder?

options.text: So you do not miss a message from the vetting team
Because the clearance decision is sent as junk mail
Because the vetting team only writes by post
Because messages are deleted after one day

questions.hint: Missing a message could delay the process.

questions.prompt: Who is the best person to ask about a delay?

options.text: Your department's security contact
A friend in another department
One of your referees, who knows you well
Your previous manager, who knows your work

questions.hint: The security contact can find out the status.

questions.prompt: Why should you not discuss your vetting details on social media?

options.text: Posts about vetting are blocked automatically
People who do not need to know should not hear them
Social media cannot display personal information about vetting
It would speed up the process

questions.hint: Vetting information is personal and should stay private.

questions.prompt: You start a new relationship while you wait for clearance. What is best?

options.text: Say nothing, because it is a private matter
Tell your department's security contact so the information is updated
Wait until your clearance is granted and mention it then, if asked
Tell your referees instead of the department

questions.hint: It is better to mention changes than to have them found.

items.title: Level 3: Security habits for new starters
items.body: Security is part of everyday work in government, and the habits you build in your first weeks matter. Many security problems are not dramatic. They are small slips, such as a laptop left on a train, a document left on a printer, or a conversation overheard in a cafe. A few simple habits reduce the risk. Lock your screen every time you leave your desk. Keep your pass on you, show it as the building rules require, and do not lend it to anyone. If a stranger is following you through a secure door, politely ask who they are and to use their own pass. This is called challenging, and it is expected. Do not talk about work in public places where others can hear. Keep papers out of sight when you are not using them, and put confidential waste in the proper bins. Use only the equipment and software the department provides, and never forward work to a personal email address. Be careful with links and attachments in emails you did not expect, because they may be attempts to steal information, known as phishing. If you notice something wrong, such as a lost pass, a missing document or a suspicious email, report it straight away to your line manager or the security team. Early reports allow harm to be limited, and nobody expects a new starter to get everything right. What matters is telling someone quickly.

items.title: Level 3: Using personal data properly
items.source: Data Protection Act 2018 and UK GDPR; GOV.UK
items.body: In many Administrative Officer jobs you handle personal information about members of the public. This can include names, addresses, dates of birth, benefit details or health information. The law that protects it is the Data Protection Act 2018, together with the UK GDPR. You do not need to know the whole law, but you need to understand the main ideas. Personal data should be used only for the purpose it was collected for. You should look at it only if your job needs you to. Looking up the record of a neighbour, a celebrity or a family member out of curiosity is a serious breach, even if you do nothing with the information. It can lead to disciplinary action and sometimes to a criminal offence. Share personal data only with people who are allowed to see it, and use the approved systems. Do not take it home on a memory stick or photograph it with your phone. Check the address before you send an email, particularly when it contains personal details. Sending a message to the wrong person is a common cause of data breaches. If you make a mistake or realise that something has gone wrong, tell your line manager or the data protection team straight away. A quick report can limit the harm, and the department would much rather hear about a mistake early than find out about it later.

questions.prompt: Which law, with UK GDPR, protects personal data in the UK?

options.text: The Official Secrets Act 1989
The Equality Act 2010
The Companies Act 2006
The Data Protection Act 2018

questions.hint: The Data Protection Act 2018 and UK GDPR protect personal data.

questions.hint: Wrong recipients cause many breaches.

questions.hint: Check the address to avoid wrong-recipient breaches.

items.title: Level 3: Speaking up and avoiding conflicts
items.body: The Civil Service Code expects you to act with integrity, and some everyday situations test this. A conflict of interest is a situation where your personal interests, or those of people close to you, could affect, or look as if they affect, your work. For example, a team member whose cousin applies for a contract the team will award has a conflict. The right step is to declare it to your manager at once so that someone else can take the decision. Declaring is not an admission of wrongdoing. It is how the system protects you. Gifts and hospitality are another area. Small items of low value may be accepted in some departments, but anything that could influence a decision should be declined and the offer recorded. Always check your department's gifts and hospitality rules. Political impartiality means that civil servants serve governments of any party. That is why you should be careful on social media and avoid posts that show strong political loyalty. If you see something wrong, such as bullying, fraud or a serious breach of the Code, you can raise a concern with your line manager or another senior person. Departments also have a route for reporting concerns in confidence. If you are not satisfied with the response, you can take the matter to the Civil Service Commission. Honest reporting is protected, and no one should be treated badly for raising a genuine concern.

options.text: A disagreement between two teams about priorities

A clash between your leave dates and a meeting

questions.hint: It covers real or apparent clashes between personal and work interests.

items.title: Level 3: Probation and the first review
items.body: Most new civil servants have a probationary period. This is a time when your manager and you check how well the job suits you and how well you suit the job. It is not a trick. Its aim is to help you succeed by giving you support, feedback and a chance to learn. During probation your manager will usually meet you regularly, agree what is expected of you, and give you feedback. You might be asked to complete mandatory learning, to show that you can do the main tasks, and to follow the Civil Service Code. Departments have written policies that set out how long probation lasts, what is looked at and what happens if there are concerns. If your manager has a worry, it should normally be discussed with you early, with time to improve. You should ask for feedback if you are not getting it. Keep notes of what you have done, such as tasks completed and training finished, so that you can talk about it at review meetings. If you have a health condition or disability that affects your work, you can ask for reasonable adjustments, which are changes that remove a disadvantage, such as different equipment or working arrangements. At the end of probation, your manager decides whether to confirm you in post. Most people who engage, ask questions and take feedback on board are confirmed.

items.title: Level 3: Records, references and the paper trail
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: Pre-employment checks leave a paper trail, and knowing what is kept helps you stay organised. When you apply, your answers form a record. Your identity documents are checked, and the employer keeps a record that the check was done, which may include a copy. The department records the result of the criminal record check, the right to work check and the employment history check. Your referees may be asked for written confirmation. All of this personal information must be stored securely and used only for the purpose of the checks and your employment. Under data protection law, you have rights over your personal data, such as the right to ask what is held about you. You can make a request to the department's data protection team. You should also keep your own records. Save the offer letter, the contract, copies of forms you submit, emails from the checks team and any reference numbers. If you move house or change your name, update the department. If a referee leaves their job or changes contact details, tell the team. A tidy set of records makes it easier to answer questions later, and it helps if you later apply for a higher level of clearance, because the same facts will need to be listed again. If two forms ever give different answers, the difference may be questioned, even when there is an innocent reason. Consistent records help avoid this.

questions.prompt: What does the employer keep when it checks your identity documents?

options.text: A photograph of your family for the file
A recording of your interview kept for years
A record that the check was done, which may include a copy

questions.hint: Records show that checks were done.

items.title: Level 3: Honesty in practice
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard, GOV.UK
items.body: Everyone agrees honesty matters, but it is easier to see what it means in practice with examples. Jo forgot a short job from two years ago. When she realises, she tells the checks team and gives the details. This is the right step. The department is likely to take a mistake that is corrected quickly as a sign that she is honest. Lee knows that a job ended badly and is tempted to leave it off. Leaving it off is a risk, because the former employer may be contacted, and a hidden job suggests he is hiding something. Better to list it and give a short, calm account. Fatima owes money and is worried. She lists the debt on a clearance questionnaire and explains she has a repayment plan. This helps, because the vetting team can see that she is dealing with it. Dev tells the department that he has lived at one address for five years, though he actually moved in the last year. When the address check shows the difference, it raises a question about honesty that could have been avoided. Across these examples, the lesson is that what damages a case is not usually the fact itself but the attempt to hide it. Honest accounts can be checked and understood. Hidden facts that appear later suggest that a person cannot be relied on. If you are uncertain, say so, and give your best answer with an explanation.

questions.prompt: What does Jo do when she realises she forgot a short job?

options.text: Tells the checks team and gives the details
Waits to see whether it is noticed
Asks her referee to mention it
Adds it after her first day without telling anyone

questions.hint: Prompt correction is the right step.

questions.prompt: Why is leaving off a job that ended badly a risk for Lee?

options.text: The department only contacts current employers
Jobs that ended badly are never counted in the history
Jobs that ended badly automatically result in refusal
The former employer may be contacted, and the gap suggests he is hiding something

questions.hint: Hidden jobs can be uncovered and look dishonest.

questions.prompt: What would be a better way for Lee to deal with the job?

options.text: List it and blame the employer in detail
List it and give a short, calm account
List it with a different name for the employer
List it with false dates

questions.hint: A short, calm account is best.

The vetting team can see she is dealing with it

questions.hint: A plan shows responsibility.

options.text: He forgot to bring a passport to the meeting
He gave an address history that the checks showed to be different
He left his referee out of the form
He moved house too often in the period

questions.hint: The mismatch raises a question about honesty.

questions.prompt: What usually damages a case most?

options.text: The fact itself
The attempt to hide a fact
The length of the form
The time the form was sent

questions.hint: Concealment is the bigger problem.

questions.prompt: What do hidden facts that appear later suggest?

options.text: That the checks were too quick
That a person cannot be relied on
That the form was too long to fill in
That the person is nervous about forms

questions.hint: They damage trust.

questions.prompt: What should you do if you are uncertain about an answer?

options.text: Choose the answer that looks best on the form

Ask a friend to answer for you

questions.hint: Honest uncertainty is acceptable.
